clue.text: Two directions to call "erratic"

parts.note: two compass points, west and east, written out with the joining word as W AND E
to call someone is to ring them on the phone

explanation.surface: Someone is told by two people at once to label something as erratic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two directions' is read literally as the phrase 'W and E', so the joining word 'and' supplies its own letters. 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something erratic is unpredictable, drifting off course, which is a synonym of roaming or straying.

clue.text: Poet showing the value of promise

indicators.note: the value of a promise is that promise's value, so the possessor comes first

parts.note: to give your word is to promise, and the 's makes it possessive
worth means value

explanation.surface: A poet demonstrates just how much a promise is worth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the value of promise' turns round to 'promise's value', a word's worth.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wordsworth was the English Romantic poet of the Lake District, an example of a poet.

clue.text: Welsh city with parking and yellow lines clear

indicators.note: the pieces before it line the word for clear, sitting inside it like a lining

parts.note: net profit is what is left clear after costs
P is the abbreviation for parking on road signs
or is the heraldic word for gold or yellow

explanation.surface: A Welsh city has parking spaces, and its yellow lines have been cleared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'yellow lines' looks like road markings, but 'yellow' is the heraldic colour and 'lines' is the container signal, putting the run before it inside the word for clear; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Newport is a city in south-east Wales, an example of a Welsh city.

clue.text: Thus regret raising some money

indicators.note: in a down clue raising means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: so means thus, as in 'and so it was'
to rue is to regret

explanation.surface: So one regrets putting up some cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raising' turns the whole run SORUE upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The euro is the currency of much of Europe, so several of them are an amount of cash.

clue.text: I demolished recent walls to put up switch

indicators.note: walls means the rebuilt letters enclose the next piece, like walls round a room
a demolished building is knocked down, so these letters are broken up and rebuilt

parts.note: to put up a picture is to hang it

explanation.surface: Someone knocks down recently built walls to put up a switch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'demolished' rearranges RECENT into NTERCE, which 'walls' round the word for put up, after the I; 'to' is a link and 'switch' is a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: An interchange is an exchange or swap, so it can stand for a switch.

clue.text: My part in stage extravaganza

indicators.note: part in says the answer is a run of letters found inside the following words

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of their role in a lavish stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive but is the exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise, as in 'My, what a show!'

clue.text: Half-heartedly shake inverted sack?

indicators.note: inverted means the trimmed word is turned the other way round
the word for shake has two letters at its heart and one of the pair is dropped, half of its heart

parts.note: to wobble is to shake

explanation.surface: Someone gives an upside-down sack a feeble shake.
explanation.walkthrough: WOBBLE loses one of its central B's to give WOBLE, which 'inverted' turns round. The question mark marks the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone the elbow is to dismiss them, so it is used loosely for firing from a job.

clue.text: Morse's first name and last always stated

indicators.note: stated means the words are heard spoken rather than read

parts.note: last means end and always means ever, said together

explanation.surface: A fan recalls the first name of Inspector Morse, always the last thing revealed.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse, the Oxford detective of British TV, kept his first name secret until late in the series. END plus EVER spoken aloud sounds like it; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspector Morse's given name, finally revealed in the books and TV series, was this word meaning an earnest attempt.

clue.text: Second-class wrench that is good for building worker

parts.note: B is the grade for second class
to rick a joint is to wrench or sprain it
IE is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A second-class spanner is said to be good enough for a builder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrench' looks like a spanner, but it is the verb, to sprain. 'good for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Brickie is British informal for bricklayer, a tradesman on a building site.

clue.text: Female unhappy about seducer

indicators.note: about means the run of letters is turned round

parts.note: low means unhappy, down in spirits

explanation.surface: A woman is downcast about the man who seduced her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns FLOW round as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A wolf is slang for a man who chases women, a womaniser.

clue.text: Perhaps stroke on back follows argument

indicators.note: follows means the reversed piece comes after the word for argument

parts.note: a row is an argument

indicators.note: back means the word for on is turned round

parts.note: re means on or concerning, as in letters

explanation.surface: A swimmer doing backstroke comes after a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stroke' and 'back' suggest swimming; stroke is the oarsman nearest the stern who sets the pace.
explanation.definitionFit: Stroke is the crew member who sets the rhythm in a racing boat, an example of an oarsman.

clue.text: Dreamt about harmful routine

indicators.note: about here means the letters are moved around into a new order

parts.note: ill means harmful, as in ill effects

explanation.surface: Someone dreamt of a damaging daily grind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges DREAMT into TREADM.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadmill is figuratively a monotonous, wearisome round of work, the same as a dull routine.

clue.text: Snow leopards vulnerable? £1000 for charity event

indicators.note: vulnerable things are easily broken, so these letters are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: K stands for a thousand, a grand

explanation.surface: Endangered snow leopards: a thousand pounds raised by a fundraiser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vulnerable' rearranges SNOWLEOPARDS, with K added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A walk whose participants are paid per mile by backers is a fundraising activity for a good cause.

clue.text: Resolution of doc he prints?

indicators.note: resolution means breaking something into its parts, so these letters are resolved into a new order

explanation.surface: A doctor wonders how sharp the documents he prints will be.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the letters of DOC HE PRINTS rearrange, and printer resolution is measured this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Printer sharpness is quoted as how many ink marks fit into each inch, a measure of image detail.

clue.text: Bright star in the sky ringed by mixture of inert gas

indicators.note: ringed by means the word for in the sky is enclosed by the rearranged letters
a mixture means these letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: something up is in the sky, aloft

explanation.surface: A bright star in the sky is surrounded by a blend of noble gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixture of' rearranges the letters of INERT GAS into SERGIANT, and 'ringed by' puts the word for aloft inside it, just after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A supergiant is among the largest and most luminous stars known, so it is a brilliant one.

clue.text: Jumbo jet finally loaded, but it can't fly

parts.note: OS is the abbreviation for outsize, jumbo

indicators.note: finally means take only the last letter of the word jet

parts.note: loaded is slang for rich

explanation.surface: A jumbo jet is at last loaded up, but it is grounded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumbo jet' suggests an aircraft; it splits into OS and the last letter of 'jet'.
explanation.definitionFit: The ostrich is the large African bird that runs but has no power of flight.

clue.text: Badger's weight? Nice one!

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, so the definition is the verb badger

parts.note: import means significance or weight, as in a matter of great import
une is French for one, as spoken in Nice on the French Riviera

explanation.surface: A badger's heaviness is admired with a cheery cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice one!' reads as praise but is the French city Nice, where 'one' is UNE. 'Badger' is the verb, to pester.
explanation.definitionFit: To importune is to pester someone persistently with requests, the same as to harass or nag.

clue.text: The pens or anything used primarily as a writer

indicators.note: pens means encloses, so the word The holds the next word inside it
primarily means take the first letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: The pens or whatever comes to hand are what a writer uses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pens' looks like writing tools, but it is the verb, to enclose; 'primarily' takes the initials of 'anything used'. 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry David Thoreau was the American author of Walden, an example of a writer.

clue.text: Rebounding shot — see another kind of shot

indicators.note: rebounding means bouncing back, so the run of letters is read backwards

parts.note: a nip is a small shot of spirits
to spot is to see

explanation.surface: A ball bounces back off one stroke; look, here comes a different stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rebounding' turns NIPSPOT round whole. The first 'shot' is a drink, the second a stroke in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: Topspin is forward rotation put on a ball in tennis or table tennis, a type of stroke.

clue.text: Cocktail stick's weight and length reduced

parts.note: a pin is something you stick into things, a cocktail stick
kg is the abbreviation for kilogram, a weight
a length of an inch, shortened to its abbreviation

explanation.surface: A cocktail stick has its weight and length cut down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cocktail stick' looks like one item; 'Cocktail' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pink gin is gin flavoured with Angostura bitters, a classic mixed drink of the Royal Navy.

clue.text: A low point for a single copy of 5

parts.note: per means for each, as in so much per head
I is the Roman numeral one
a repeat of the answer to clue 5 down

explanation.surface: One copy of clue five gives a low point.
explanation.walkthrough: The '5' refers to the answer at 5 down, the exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: The perigee is where an orbiting body comes nearest the earth, the lowest point of its orbit.

clue.text: Good pepper to cook

parts.note: to pepper with bullets is to riddle with holes

explanation.surface: A good pepper is needed for cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pepper' looks like the spice, but it is the verb, to spray with shot.
explanation.definitionFit: To griddle food is to fry or grill it on a flat iron plate, a way to prepare a meal.

clue.text: Apt to worry crew, given rank at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A ship's crew handed a rank at sea is likely to fret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' rearranges CREW GIVEN RANK together.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nerve-wracking causes stress and anxiety, so it is likely to cause concern.

clue.text: Club's extra security

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
over means extra or surplus, as in left over

explanation.surface: A club asks for additional safety measures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extra cover' is also a fielding position in cricket, a deliberate distraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Insurance cover gives protection against loss, a form of financial safety.

clue.text: Surrounded by the morning papers

parts.note: AM is the abbreviation for ante meridiem, before noon
ID means identity papers

explanation.surface: Someone sits buried in the morning newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'papers' suggests newspapers but means identity documents.
explanation.definitionFit: Amid means in the middle of, encircled by things.

clue.text: He asked questions — samsung moved forward

indicators.note: moved means the letters are shifted into a new order

parts.note: on means forward, as in moving on

explanation.surface: A quizmaster notes that Samsung has made progress.
explanation.walkthrough: Magnus Magnusson hosted Mastermind, a long-running British TV quiz. 'moved' rearranges SAMSUNG into MAGNUSS.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnus Magnusson was the Icelandic-born host of BBC TV quiz Mastermind, famous for posing them.

clue.text: Son and father in bath

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A boy and his dad share a bathtub.
explanation.definitionFit: Bath in Somerset is a famous English town with hot springs, the classic example of a health resort.

clue.text: Russian tipple, spirit associated with very excessive intake

parts.note: OD is an overdose, too much of a drug taken
ka is the ancient Egyptian word for the soul or spirit

explanation.surface: A Russian drink is a spirit tied to heavy drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spirit' looks like part of the definition, a strong drink, but it is KA, placed last; 'associated with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Vodka is the clear distilled spirit traditionally drunk in Russia, its national drink.

clue.text: Heavy part of garden seat

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A garden bench is a weighty piece of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dense is thick and compact, so it weighs a lot for its size.

clue.text: A wicked brother admitting name is hateful

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so the rearranged letters take in the next piece
wicked means bad or twisted, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wicked brother who takes someone's name is detestable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wicked' rearranges BROTHER into BHORRET, and 'admitting' puts N inside it; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something abhorrent inspires disgust and loathing, so it is detestable.
